How artificial intelligence is changing protein design

Published 2026-10-07 02:30 UTC

For decades, designing a new protein meant starting from one found in nature and changing it a little at a time. Generative artificial intelligence models have upended that process. Researchers can now ask a model for a protein with a particular shape or function and receive designs for molecules that have never existed.

The models learn from databases of known protein structures and sequences. Some generate a three-dimensional backbone first and then choose an amino acid sequence that will fold into it. Others generate sequences directly. In both cases, scientists then make the proteins in the lab to see whether they work.

The results have been striking. Labs have used the methods to design enzymes that speed up chemical reactions not catalyzed by any natural protein, binders that latch onto viral proteins, and molecular switches that change shape when they encounter a specific signal. Success rates in the lab, once a few percent, now often exceed 20 percent for some kinds of designs.

Researchers caution that the models are best at shapes, not chemistry. An enzyme needs atoms positioned precisely to break and form bonds, and designed enzymes are usually far less efficient than natural ones at first. Labs still rely on rounds of directed evolution, mutating and selecting the best variants, to improve them.

The speed of progress has also raised concerns about misuse. Several groups have proposed screening systems for DNA synthesis orders and model outputs to flag designs resembling toxins. Scientists in the field have signed commitments to responsible development, though how to enforce them remains unsettled.

For many biochemists, the change is philosophical as well as practical. The space of possible proteins is vastly larger than what evolution has explored, and AI models offer a way to map parts of it that nature never reached.
